tip: Luggage is uncountable in English but plural in French: les bagages always takes a plural article and verb. One bag alone is un bagage.
Son doesn't show the owner's gender – it agrees with the noun. Anniversaire is masculine, so son anniversaire is his OR her birthday alike.
Récupérer looks like 'recuperate' but here means to collect or pick up: nous récupérons les valises = we get the suitcases back, not we recover from them.
French marries reflexively: se marier, literally 'to marry oneself'. Ils se marieront = they'll get married. Without se, marier means to marry someone else off.
No word for 'on' with days: seront publiés vendredi = will be published on Friday. Add le – le vendredi – and it flips to mean every Friday.
Visiter is for places, not people: nous visiterons la Bretagne. To visit a person you say rendre visite à, never visiter quelqu'un.
Age is something you have in French: elle aura trente ans = literally 'she will have thirty years'. Using être here is a classic English-speaker slip.
Travail becomes travaux in the plural, and les travaux specifically means construction or renovation work: finir les travaux = finish the building work.
After dès que, French uses the future where English keeps the present: elle sera prête = literally 'she will be ready'. Both clauses go future.
Aurais voulu expresses regret about the past: j'aurais voulu être là = I would have liked to be there, meaning I wish I had been but wasn't.
You take a decision in French, not make one: nous prendrons une décision = we'll make a decision. Using faire here would sound wrong.
Décevoir means to disappoint, not to deceive – a false friend. Je ne te décevrai pas = I won't let you down. To deceive someone is tromper.
Essence looks like the English 'essence' but means gasoline: on va prendre de l'essence = we'll get fuel. Perfume is un parfum, not essence.
Manquer reverses things: tu nous manqueras = literally 'you will be missing to us'. The person missed is the subject, so tu me manques means 'I miss you'.
Réussir l'examen means to pass the exam, not merely to succeed: qui ont réussi l'examen = who passed it. To fail it is rater or échouer à.
Demander means to ask for, not to demand: demander une augmentation = to ask for a raise. And you ask it à someone – demander à mon patron.
No 'a' before a profession after être: je serais médecin = I'd be a doctor. You only add un when you describe it – un bon médecin.
Il faudra has no real subject – il is a dummy placeholder: il faudra se remettre au travail = 'one will have to' get back to work. It comes from falloir.
S'occuper always needs de for what you handle: qui s'occupe de mon père = who takes care of my father. Drop the de and the sentence breaks.
Assister à means to attend, not to assist – a false friend: assister à la réunion = to be at the meeting. To help someone is aider.
For an action finished before another future one, French uses the future perfect: aurons vendu = will have sold. English just says 'have sold'.
French uses the present with depuis for something still going on: attend depuis une heure = has been waiting for an hour, and still is.
Si never takes a conditional verb – the setup stays imparfait: même si j'avais... je ne l'achèterais pas = even if I had... I wouldn't buy it.
